warmup.q: A virtual thread prints Thread.currentThread(), sleeps for 50 ms, and prints it again. What do you expect to see?
options: The same platform thread both times, because a thread can't change its OS thread
The same virtual thread both times, possibly running on a different carrier thread after the sleep
Two different virtual threads, because the JDK creates a new one after each blocking call
The carrier thread, because currentThread() returns the OS thread that is running the code
warmup.why: Thread.currentThread() always returns the virtual thread itself, never its carrier. During the sleep the virtual thread is unmounted, and when it wakes, any free carrier can pick it up. The virtual thread's toString() shows the current carrier after the @, which is how the demo in this lesson makes the switch visible.

sections.h: A virtual thread is a Thread plus a continuation
sections.html:
Thread.ofVirtual().start(task) returns an ordinary java.lang.Thread. Inside the JDK it is an instance of java.lang.VirtualThread, a package-private subclass. It holds two things a platform thread doesn't have: a continuation and a scheduler.

A continuation is a paused piece of code: everything a computation still has to do, plus every stack frame it had when it stopped. The JDK has an internal class for it, jdk.internal.vm.Continuation, with two operations that matter. run() starts the code, or resumes it where it stopped. yield(), called from inside that code, stops it and returns control to whoever called run(), with the frames kept. The next run() carries on from the line after the yield().

cont = new Continuation(scope, () -> { a(); yield(); b(); })
cont.run()    // runs a(), stops at yield(), returns here
cont.run()    // carries on with b()

You can't call this class yourself: the jdk.internal.vm package is not exported. The virtual thread uses it for you. Its task is wrapped in a continuation, and when the task is about to block, the JDK calls yield(). The thread stops without ever blocking an OS thread.

The scheduler decides which paused continuation runs next, and on which OS thread.

To your code, a virtual thread is just a thread. Thread.currentThread() returns it. ThreadLocals work. interrupt() works, and sleep throws InterruptedException the same way. Stack traces show your frames. A few things differ, and they are all in the Thread Javadoc: virtual threads are always daemon threads, their priority is fixed, they have no name unless you give one, and Thread.getAllStackTraces() leaves them out.

Check yourself: a virtual thread runs a task that sleeps three times and then returns. How many times does its continuation yield, and how many times does a carrier mount it? It yields three times, once per sleep. It is mounted four times: once to start, and once after each sleep ends.

sections.h: Carriers: a few platform threads run every virtual thread
sections.html:
The default scheduler is a ForkJoinPool that the JDK creates just for virtual threads. It is a different pool from ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which parallel streams use. It runs in FIFO mode, so ready virtual threads run roughly in the order they became ready.

Its worker threads are platform threads, and they have a special name: carrier threads. By default there is one per core (Runtime.availableProcessors()). You can change that with -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=N. The pool may add carriers for a while when some operation blocks a carrier, up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize, which defaults to 256.

Two words describe the life of a virtual thread on a carrier:

  • Mount: a carrier takes a ready virtual thread from the queue and runs its continuation. The virtual thread's top frames are now on the carrier's stack, and the carrier is busy running your code.
  • Unmount: the continuation yields at a blocking call. The frames go to the heap, and the carrier goes back to the pool to mount someone else.

The carrier is invisible to your code. Thread.currentThread() returns the virtual thread, and the carrier's own ThreadLocals are not visible. The one place it shows is the virtual thread's toString(): VirtualThread[#22,payment-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3. The part after @ is the carrier. Treat that format as a debugging aid, not an API: it is not specified anywhere.

A virtual thread that unmounts can come back on any carrier. That is normal, and it is why the JDK never lets your code see the carrier: a ThreadLocal on the carrier would leak between unrelated requests.

try.title: Watch virtual threads change carriers
steps: Run CarrierDemo with the command below. It starts 8 virtual threads that print Thread.currentThread(), sleep 50 ms, and print it again.
Count the carriers in the summary line and compare with your number of cores. How many threads woke up on a different carrier?
Predict, then run with one carrier: -Pargs='8 1'. Does it take 8 times as long?

code.title: CarrierDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeSet; /** * Starts some virtual threads that each print the thread they run on, sleep, and print it again. * A virtual thread's toString() shows its carrier after the '@'. * * <p>Args: number of virtual threads (default 8), and optionally the scheduler's parallelism. */ public class CarrierDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int n = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 8; if (args.length > 1) { // must be set before the first virtual thread is created System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", args[1]); } String[] before = new String[n]; String[] after = new String[n]; List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int id = i; threads.add(Thread.ofVirtual().name("payment-" + id).start(() -> { before[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString(); try { Thread.sleep(50); // a blocking call: the thread unmounts here } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } after[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString(); })); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; Set<String> carriers = new TreeSet<>(); int moved = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { System.out.printf("before: %-63s after: %s%n", before[i], after[i]); carriers.add(carrier(before[i])); carriers.add(carrier(after[i])); if (!carrier(before[i]).equals(carrier(after[i]))) moved++; } System.out.printf("%n%d virtual threads ran on %d carrier threads %s (this machine has %d cores).%n", n, carriers.size(), carriers, Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); System.out.printf("%d of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on.%n", moved); System.out.printf("All %d finished after %d ms.%n", n, ms); System.out.println("Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() inside them: " + threads.get(0).isVirtual() + ", daemon: " + threads.get(0).isDaemon()); } // "VirtualThread[#22,payment-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" -> "ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" static String carrier(String s) { int at = s.lastIndexOf('@'); return at < 0 ? "(not mounted)" : s.substring(at + 1); } }

alt.title: CarrierDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02 import java.util.TreeSet /** * Starts some virtual threads that each print the thread they run on, sleep, and print it again. * A virtual thread's toString() shows its carrier after the '@'. * * Args: number of virtual threads (default 8), and optionally the scheduler's parallelism. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val n = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 8 // must be set before the first virtual thread is created args.getOrNull(1)?.let { System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", it) } val before = arrayOfNulls<String>(n) val after = arrayOfNulls<String>(n) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = (0 until n).map { id -> Thread.ofVirtual().name("payment-$id").start { before[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString() try { Thread.sleep(50) // a blocking call: the thread unmounts here } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } after[id] = Thread.currentThread().toString() } } threads.forEach { it.join() } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val carriers = TreeSet<String>() var moved = 0 for (i in 0 until n) { println("before: %-63s after: %s".format(before[i], after[i])) carriers += carrierOf(before[i]!!) carriers += carrierOf(after[i]!!) if (carrierOf(before[i]!!) != carrierOf(after[i]!!)) moved++ } println("\n$n virtual threads ran on ${carriers.size} carrier threads $carriers (this machine has ${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()} cores).") println("$moved of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on.") println("All $n finished after $ms ms.") println("Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() inside them: ${threads[0].isVirtual}, daemon: ${threads[0].isDaemon}") } // "VirtualThread[#22,payment-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" -> "ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3" private fun carrierOf(s: String): String { val at = s.lastIndexOf('@') return if (at < 0) "(not mounted)" else s.substring(at + 1) }

try.expect: On a 4-core machine all 8 virtual threads share carriers worker-1 to worker-4, and most of them wake up on a different carrier than they slept on (7 of 8 in one run here). With one carrier everything shows worker-1, and it still finishes in about 50 ms plus startup: the 8 sleeps overlap, because a sleeping virtual thread doesn't hold the carrier.

video.title: Virtual threads mount on carriers, unmount at a blocking call, and come back on any carrier

sections.h: Blocking points: where a virtual thread lets go
sections.html:
Unmounting is not magic in the JVM. The JDK team rewrote the blocking parts of the class library to check whether the current thread is virtual, and to yield instead of blocking. Here is parkNanos from java.lang.VirtualThread, trimmed to its core:

// simplified from java.lang.VirtualThread.parkNanos (JDK 25)
void parkNanos(long nanos) {
    timeout = nanos;
    setState(TIMED_PARKING);
    boolean yielded = yieldContinuation();   // unmount: frames to the heap, carrier is free
    if (!yielded) {
        parkOnCarrierThread(true, nanos);    // couldn't unmount: block the carrier instead
    }
}

The JDK schedules a timer that will unpark the thread, and yieldContinuation() unmounts it. When the timer fires, the virtual thread goes back into the scheduler's queue.

These operations unmount a virtual thread:

  • Thread.sleep and LockSupport.park, and everything built on park: ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch, BlockingQueue.take, Future.get, CompletableFuture.join.
  • Socket I/O, including the JDK's HttpClient and JDBC drivers that use plain sockets. The JDK switches the socket to non-blocking mode and registers it with a poller (epoll on Linux), which unparks the virtual thread when data arrives.
  • From JDK 24 (JEP 491), synchronized and Object.wait(). On JDK 21 to 23 these pin the carrier instead: the virtual thread stays mounted, and the carrier blocks with it. Lesson 4 of this track covers that.

Some operations can't unmount. Most file I/O blocks inside the OS, so the JDK lets it take over the carrier ("capture") and adds a temporary extra carrier to make up for it. Blocking while a native method or a class initializer is on the stack pins the carrier.

The last rule surprises people: there is no time slicing. A virtual thread that computes for two seconds without blocking keeps its carrier for two seconds. Other virtual threads wait for a free carrier. Virtual threads are cheap waiting, not cheap computing.

try.title: Replace the sleep with real work
steps: In CarrierDemo.java, replace Thread.sleep(50); with a 50 ms busy loop: long end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }. The compiler will then complain about the unreachable catch, so remove the try and catch too. In CarrierDemo.kt the loop is val end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }, and Kotlin doesn't mind the leftover catch.
Predict the total time with one carrier (-Pargs='8 1') and with the default number of carriers. Then run both.
Look at the before and after carriers. Did any thread change carrier this time?
try.expect: With one carrier the 8 busy loops run one after another: about 400 ms. With 4 carriers it takes about 100 ms on an idle machine (8 loops / 4 carriers x 50 ms), more if other programs are busy. No thread changes carrier, because none of them ever blocks, so none of them unmounts. CPU work is limited by carriers, which means cores.

sections.html:
A platform thread's stack is a fixed block of native memory reserved when the thread starts, 1 MB by default. A virtual thread's stack is different. When it unmounts, the JDK copies its frames off the carrier's stack into stack chunk objects on the Java heap. The chunk is only as big as the frames that are really there, and the garbage collector manages it like any other object.

When the virtual thread mounts again, the JDK doesn't copy the whole stack back. It copies the top few frames, enough to continue. If your code returns into a frame that is still on the heap, the JDK copies more at that point. A thread parked deep inside a framework pays for its depth only once, when it parks.

This is what makes a million virtual threads possible. A virtual thread parked at a shallow depth costs about 2 KB of heap in the demo below, including the Thread object. A thread parked 200 frames deep costs more, because each frame has to be stored. Deep framework stacks (a Quarkus REST call through several interceptors, a Hibernate query) are not free, but they are paid for in heap, which the GC can reclaim, not in reserved memory sized for the worst case.

It also explains a design choice. Kotlin coroutines save only the locals of suspend functions, in objects the compiler generates. A virtual thread saves the whole real stack, so a blocking call deep inside a library that knows nothing about virtual threads can still unmount. The compare block below shows both.

In the lab you build the other half: a tiny scheduler with a run queue, a timer queue and one carrier, which mounts and unmounts hand-written continuations.

try.title: Weigh a parked virtual thread
steps: Run StackOnHeapDemo. It parks 10,000 virtual threads at call depth 1, measures the heap, releases them, then does the same at depth 200.
Before you look: how many times bigger will the depth-200 number be?
Run -Pargs=1000 for depth 1,000 and compare with the 1 MB a platform thread reserves.

code.title: StackOnHeapDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * Parks 10,000 virtual threads at a chosen call depth and measures how much heap they use. * A parked virtual thread keeps its stack frames in heap objects, so deeper stacks cost more heap. * * <p>Args: call depth before parking (default: runs 1 and 200). */ public class StackOnHeapDemo { static final int THREADS = 10_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int[] depths = args.length > 0 ? new int[] {Integer.parseInt(args[0])} : new int[] {1, 200}; for (int depth : depths) measure(depth); } static void measure(int depth) throws InterruptedException { long base = usedHeap(); CountDownLatch parked = new CountDownLatch(THREADS); CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(THREADS); for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) { threads.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> descend(depth, parked, release))); } parked.await(); // every thread is now parked at the bottom of its stack long used = usedHeap() - base; System.out.printf("depth %3d: %,d parked virtual threads use about %,d MB of heap (%,d bytes each)%n", depth, THREADS, used / (1024 * 1024), used / THREADS); release.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); } // each level adds one stack frame; at the bottom the thread blocks and unmounts static int descend(int depth, CountDownLatch parked, CountDownLatch release) { if (depth > 1) return descend(depth - 1, parked, release) + 1; parked.countDown(); try { release.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return 0; } static long usedHeap() throws InterruptedException { Runtime rt = Runtime.getRuntime(); for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(50); } return rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory(); } }

alt.title: StackOnHeapDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l02 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch /** * Parks 10,000 virtual threads at a chosen call depth and measures how much heap they use. * A parked virtual thread keeps its stack frames in heap objects, so deeper stacks cost more heap. * * Args: call depth before parking (default: runs 1 and 200). */ private const val THREADS = 10_000 fun main(args: Array<String>) { val depths = args.getOrNull(0)?.let { listOf(it.toInt()) } ?: listOf(1, 200) for (depth in depths) measure(depth) } private fun measure(depth: Int) { val base = usedHeap() val parked = CountDownLatch(THREADS) val release = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(THREADS) { Thread.ofVirtual().start { descend(depth, parked, release) } } parked.await() // every thread is now parked at the bottom of its stack val used = usedHeap() - base println("depth %3d: %,d parked virtual threads use about %,d MB of heap (%,d bytes each)" .format(depth, THREADS, used / (1024 * 1024), used / THREADS)) release.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } } // each level adds one stack frame; at the bottom the thread blocks and unmounts private fun descend(depth: Int, parked: CountDownLatch, release: CountDownLatch): Int { if (depth > 1) return descend(depth - 1, parked, release) + 1 parked.countDown() try { release.await() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } return 0 } private fun usedHeap(): Long { val rt = Runtime.getRuntime() repeat(2) { System.gc() Thread.sleep(50) } return rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory() }

try.expect: At depth 1 each parked virtual thread costs about 2 KB of heap. At depth 200 it costs about 10 to 15 KB, depending on the JDK and on whether the JIT compiled descend yet. Even at depth 1,000 it stays far below 1 MB. The heap grows with the real depth of the stack, nothing more. The numbers are rough because totalMemory - freeMemory after System.gc() is a rough measure.

analogy: Think of carriers as desks in an office and virtual threads as workers who carry their papers in a briefcase. A worker sits at any free desk and spreads out the papers. When the worker has to wait for a phone call, they pack everything into the briefcase, put it on a shelf, and free the desk. When the call comes, they take the next free desk, which may be a different one, and carry on. There are only as many desks as cores, but there can be a million briefcases on the shelves. The analogy breaks in one place: a real worker can be told to leave the desk. A virtual thread that never waits for anything keeps its desk until it is done, because nobody makes it get up.
world: When you take a thread dump of a Quarkus service on virtual threads, the carriers show up as ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N platform threads, mostly idle, and jstack shows the carriers but not the parked virtual threads. Use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json to see them. The no-time-slicing rule matters for payment code: a virtual thread that verifies a large batch of signatures or parses a 50 MB settlement file holds a carrier the whole time. Four of those on a 4-core pod and every HTTP request waits. Keep heavy CPU work on a bounded platform pool, and keep virtual threads for code that waits.
mistake: The most common mistake is believing a virtual thread runs on "its" OS thread, and writing code that depends on that: carrier-level ThreadLocal tricks, native libraries that keep state per OS thread, or logging the OS thread id to correlate requests. A virtual thread can resume on a different carrier after every blocking call, and the JDK hides the carrier on purpose. Correlate with the virtual thread (or better, a request id you pass along), and treat the carrier as an implementation detail you never touch.

compare.title: Stackful virtual threads vs stackless coroutines

java.title: Java: the JDK saves the real stack
java.html: // any method can block, even deep inside an old library void settle(Payment p) throws InterruptedException { Auth auth = issuer.authorize(p); // blocking socket read: unmounts here Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(30)); // unmounts here too ledger.record(p, auth); // plain JDBC over a socket: unmounts } // run it on a virtual thread; nothing in settle() knows Thread.ofVirtual().name("settle-", 0).start(() -> { try { settle(payment); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } });

kotlin.title: Kotlin: the compiler builds a state machine
kotlin.html: // only suspend calls can pause; the compiler rewrites this function suspend fun settle(p: Payment) { val auth = issuer.authorize(p) // must be a suspend fun to free the thread delay(30) ledger.record(p, auth) // blocking JDBC here would block the thread } // roughly what the compiler generates (simplified): // class SettleContinuation(var label: Int, var auth: Auth?) // label 0: call authorize(p); label = 1; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 1: auth = result; call delay(30); label = 2; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 2: ledger.record(p, auth)

compare.note: Both pause in the middle of a function and continue later, possibly on another thread. Kotlin coroutines are stackless: the compiler turns each suspend function into a state machine and saves its locals in a generated continuation object, so only suspend calls can pause. Virtual threads are stackful: the JVM copies the real frames, so any blocking JDK call anywhere on the stack can unmount, including calls inside libraries compiled before virtual threads existed. The fibers in this lesson's lab are written by hand in the Kotlin style, with a label counter, so you can see what the JDK saves you from writing.

worked.title: Follow one virtual thread through a sleep

steps.say: Here is the task. The comments mark the points where the virtual thread's life changes.
steps.code: Thread vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-1").start(() -> { // 1. start: queued in the scheduler Risk risk = fraud.check(payment); // 2. mounted on some carrier, say worker-2 sleepQuietly(Duration.ofMillis(50)); // 3. unmounts here; worker-2 is free issuer.authorize(payment, risk); // 4. resumed, maybe on worker-4 });

alt.html: val vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-1").start { // 1. start: queued in the scheduler val risk = fraud.check(payment) // 2. mounted on some carrier, say worker-2 Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(50)) // 3. unmounts here; worker-2 is free issuer.authorize(payment, risk) // 4. resumed, maybe on worker-4 }

steps.say: Start. start() doesn't run anything on the caller's thread. It submits the virtual thread's continuation to the scheduler's queue as a task. The caller carries on at once.

Mount. A free carrier, worker-2, takes the task and calls run() on the continuation. The frames of the lambda and of fraud.check are on worker-2's stack now. Inside, Thread.currentThread() is auth-1. The socket reads inside fraud.check may unmount and remount it several times on their own.

Unmount. sleep reaches parkNanos, which schedules a timer for 50 ms and calls yieldContinuation(). The JDK copies the frames into a stack chunk on the heap, and run() returns on worker-2. worker-2 goes back to the queue and mounts another virtual thread. No OS thread is blocked.

Wake and remount. The timer fires and unparks auth-1, which puts its continuation back in the queue. Whichever carrier is free next, say worker-4, mounts it, copies the top frames back, and sleep returns. The code runs issuer.authorize without knowing it moved.

lab.title: Build a one-carrier scheduler
steps: Read Fiber and Step. A Fiber is a hand-written continuation: each resume() runs to the next blocking point and returns Step.Sleep(ms) or Step.Done. You don't change these two files.
Run the tests once. All six fail. Read ToySchedulerTest.sleeper: it is a fiber written as a state machine with a program counter, like a Kotlin suspend function.
In ToyScheduler, add a run queue (ArrayDeque<Fiber>), a timer queue (PriorityQueue of a small record holding the wake-up time, a sequence number and the fiber), and a long now.

Write run() as one loop that runs while either queue has something: if nothing is ready, jump now to the earliest wake-up and move every fiber due at that time into the run queue. Then take one ready fiber, count a mount, call resume(), and park it in the timer queue if it asked to sleep.
Run the tests until all six pass. Look at the 10,000-fiber test: 30,000 mounts on one thread, and the clock ends at 150 ms.
hints: Order the timer queue by wake-up time, then by a sequence number you increment on every park. That keeps fibers that wake at the same moment in the order they went to sleep.
Java 21 can switch on the sealed Step: switch (step) { case Step.Sleep s -> ...; case Step.Done d -> { } }. The compiler checks that you covered both.
Move fibers from the timer queue only when the run queue is empty. Running code takes no virtual time, so the clock only moves when nothing can run.

drill.title: The scheduler loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. On paper or in a blank file, write the body of run(): a run queue, a timer queue ordered by wake-up time, a virtual clock, and the mount and unmount steps. Then label each part with the real thing it stands for in the JDK (the ForkJoinPool queue, the carrier, yield(), the timer that unparks a sleeping thread).

answer.html: int mounts = 0; while (!ready.isEmpty() || !sleeping.isEmpty()) { if (ready.isEmpty()) { // JDK: carriers idle, waiting for events now = sleeping.peek().wakeAt(); while (!sleeping.isEmpty() && sleeping.peek().wakeAt() <= now) { ready.addLast(sleeping.poll().fiber()); // JDK: the timer unparks, thread is resubmitted } } Fiber f = ready.pollFirst(); // JDK: a carrier takes the next task (FIFO) mounts++; Step step = f.resume(); // JDK: mount, Continuation.run() if (step instanceof Step.Sleep s) { // JDK: Continuation.yield() at sleep, unmount sleeping.add(new Parked(now + s.millis(), seq++, f)); } } return mounts;

alt.html: var mounts = 0 while (ready.isNotEmpty() || sleeping.isNotEmpty()) { if (ready.isEmpty()) { // JDK: carriers idle, waiting for events now = sleeping.peek().wakeAt while (sleeping.isNotEmpty() && sleeping.peek().wakeAt <= now) { ready.addLast(sleeping.poll().fiber) // JDK: the timer unparks, thread is resubmitted } } val f = ready.removeFirst() // JDK: a carrier takes the next task (FIFO) mounts++ when (val step = f.resume()) { // JDK: mount, Continuation.run() is Step.Sleep -> sleeping.add(Parked(now + step.millis(), seq++, f)) // JDK: yield() at sleep, unmount is Step.Done -> {} } } return mounts

recap: A virtual thread is a Thread whose task runs inside a continuation: code that can stop at yield() and resume later with its frames intact.
Carrier threads are the platform workers of a dedicated ForkJoinPool, one per core by default. Mount means a carrier runs the virtual thread; unmount means it lets go at a blocking call.
Thread.currentThread() always returns the virtual thread. A virtual thread may resume on a different carrier after every blocking call.
Sleep, park (locks, queues, latches, futures) and socket I/O unmount. synchronized unmounts from JDK 24 only. File I/O captures the carrier, and native frames pin it.
There is no time slicing: a virtual thread that computes keeps its carrier until it blocks or ends.
A parked virtual thread's frames live on the heap in stack chunks sized to the real depth, about 2 KB for a shallow stack.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "If a virtual thread is a real Thread, how can a million of them run on 8 OS threads? Doesn't Thread.sleep block the OS thread?" Explain what happens to a virtual thread when it sleeps.
explain.answer: A virtual thread runs its task inside a continuation, on a carrier thread taken from a small ForkJoinPool, about one per core. When the code calls sleep, the JDK sees that the current thread is virtual. It sets a timer and yields the continuation: the stack frames are copied to the heap and the carrier goes back to run another virtual thread. No OS thread waits. When the timer fires, the virtual thread goes back into the queue, and whichever carrier is free mounts it, copies the top frames back, and sleep returns. So a million sleeping virtual threads are a million small heap objects, and only the ones actually running need a carrier. The same happens for socket reads, locks and queues, but not for long CPU work, which keeps the carrier until it finishes.

deeper.html:
Three implementation details are worth knowing, because they explain behavior you will see in production.

How sockets unmount. A socket used from a virtual thread is put in non-blocking mode. When a read would block, the JDK registers the socket's file descriptor with a poller (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS) and parks the virtual thread. The poller waits on all the registered sockets at once and unparks each virtual thread when its socket is ready. One OS-level wait covers thousands of connections, which is what event-loop frameworks do by hand.

Why file I/O is different. Linux has no general non-blocking API for regular files that the JDK uses here, so a file read really blocks the OS thread. The JDK lets the virtual thread capture its carrier for the duration and asks the scheduler for a temporary extra carrier so the others keep running. That is why jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize exists. A service that does heavy file I/O on virtual threads can see the carrier count grow toward 256.

Why FIFO. A ForkJoinPool normally runs a worker's own tasks last-in first-out, which is good for divide-and-conquer work. For virtual threads the JDK creates it in async mode, which is first-in first-out, so a virtual thread that became ready long ago runs before one that became ready a moment ago. That keeps latency fair across requests.

The scheduler itself is not a public API in JDK 21 or 25. You can tune its size with the system properties, but you can't plug in your own scheduler. Libraries that need special scheduling still use platform threads.
